title: Writing an Iterator

writing.exampleCaption: Only `next` is written; `take` and `sum` come for free.
writing.explanation:
`Iterator` requires only next(); everything else — map, filter, take, zip, sum — arrives as default methods. That is why a custom sequence composes with the standard library exactly like a `Vec` does, without any of it knowing your type exists.

Implementing `Iterator` means defining the type of each item and one method, `next`. Each call either returns `Some(item)` and advances internal state or returns `None` when the sequence is finished. The default adapters then work automatically because they are expressed in terms of repeated `next` calls. That is the core composability advantage: your `Fibonacci` can be filtered, zipped, limited, and summed like an iterator from the standard library.

Walk through the sample with initial `a` and `b` values. Record the returned `value` before updating the state, then compute the pair for the next call. Test the first six outputs by hand. For an unbounded sequence, a consumer like `collect::<Vec<_>>()` would never finish; use `.take(n)` or another finite stopping rule. Also consider arithmetic overflow: with `u64`, sufficiently large Fibonacci numbers exceed the type. Decide whether `next` should stop with `None`, use checked addition, or deliberately wrap, and document that choice.

A good custom iterator keeps `next` small and makes its state invariant clear. If the sequence owns its data, consuming it may be natural; if callers need the source afterward, return an iterator that borrows it. Implement `size_hint` only when you can provide a truthful bound. The small required interface is powerful, but correctness of state transitions remains your responsibility.

`None` normally means the sequence has ended. Consumers may ask for `next()` again, so document whether your iterator stays finished; implementing `FusedIterator` is an additional promise only when that behavior is guaranteed. Test the terminal state and any overflow boundary, not merely the first few values.

A final call after completion should have a documented outcome.
writing.feedback: `None` ends the iteration, and every adapter respects it.
writing.question: What signals that the sequence has finished?
